title: Strain-transfer at the Cu nanoparticle-Si(111) interface: static atomistic modelling and simulated Bragg CDI
abstract: arXiv:2611.28036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Substrate strain offers a route to control deformation in supported metallic nanoparticles, provided that interfacial coupling transmits the imposed loading into the particle. We assess this feasibility using five static Cu/Si(111) configurations spanning 0-2% biaxial tensile substrate strain. A 211,288-atom Cu particle is supported by a nominally 50 x 50 x 20 nm Si slab with its bottom 1 nm fixed, using the Jelinek modified embeddedatom potential. Relative to the relaxed supported 0% state, Cu-only local fits reveal heterogeneous, anisotropic deformation: particle-wide mean hydrostatic strain is negative at every nonzero loading, from -3.12 x 10-6 to -8.84 x 10-6, while the upper-particle mean varies nonmonotonically. Simulated Bragg CDI of Cu(111), obtained by inversion of known complex atomic scattering amplitudes, maps loading-dependent projected displacement and strain. The combined atomistic and Bragg CDI representations provide strong preliminary support for the feasibility of substrate-mediated strain transfer in this idealized system and identify spatial signatures for experimental investigation. Experiments remain indispensable to confirm transfer in real Cu/Si(111) nanoparticles and determine its magnitude.
summary:
- Static atomistic models show strain transfer from 0–2 % biaxial tensile Si(to a 211 k‑atom Cu nanoparticle.
- Cu deformation is heterogeneous and anisotropic; mean hydrostatic strain is negative (≈ –3 to –9 ppm) and upper‑particle strain varies non‑monotonically.
- Simulated Bragg CDI yields projected displacement/strain maps, providing spatial signatures for experimental confirmation.

title: From raw magnetoresistance to reliable cyclotron masses: A practical guide to processing quantum oscillation data
authors: Josh Leeman, Sudipta Chatterjee, Max Hirschberger, Leslie M. Schoop
abstract: arXiv:2611.28044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum oscillations are an essential probe of the Fermi surface in conductors, and cyclotron masses extracted using the Lifshitz-Kosevich (LK) formula are used to evaluate correlation strength and the assignment of topological states. These masses depend on choices in signal processing, including the field window, method of background subtraction, and spectral window applied before the Fourier transform. These choices are often guided by visual inspection, yet they can alter spectral features and bias the extracted masses. We show that (1) representing a finite field interval by a single effective field can underestimate the cyclotron mass; (2) polynomial background subtraction can attenuate and shift low-frequency peaks; and (3) spectral tapering can reduce mass bias from leakage between neighboring peaks, at the cost of frequency resolution. We demonstrate these effects using numerical calculations and Shubnikov-de Haas experiments on the rare-earth tritellurides RTe3 (R = Pr, Nd, Gd, Tb) with a dense low-frequency spectrum in the charge ordered state. The examples reveal masses shifting by tens of percent with the field window, apparent peak shifts produced only by the background fit, and a reported departure from LK behavior that resolves into two neighboring frequencies.
summary:
- Finite‑field intervals misrepresented by a single effective field underestimate cyclotron masses.
- Polynomial background subtraction attenuates and shifts low‑frequency peaks, biasing mass extraction.
- Spectral tapering reduces leakage‑induced mass bias at the cost of frequency resolution, as shown in RTe₃ experiments.

title: Particle separation in a time-correlated Gaussian velocity field: a numerical study
abstract: arXiv:2611.28147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We numerically investigate the dispersion of passive tracer pairs in a two-dimensional, divergence-free, time-correlated Gaussian velocity field. The field is constructed from a sparse set of Fourier modes evolving as independent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes, with spatial regularity and scale-dependent temporal decorrelation comparable to those of a power-law Gaussian velocity ensemble. We show that, for spatial roughness exponent $\alpha=0.2$ and temporal decorrelation exponent $\beta=0.5$, corresponding to the regime $\alpha+\beta<1$, the extrapolated mean-square distance is compatible with particle separation (in mean-square) at positive time: two particles reach a mean-square positive distance at a finite time, no matter how close they are initially.
summary:
- Numerical study of passive tracer pair dispersion in a 2D, divergence‑free, time‑correlated Gaussian velocity field.
- Velocity field built from sparse Fourier modes evolving as independent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, matching power‑law spatial roughness (α = and temporal decorrelation (β = .
- In the α + β < 1 regime, mean‑square separation grows from any initial proximity, reaching a finite positive distance in finite time.

title: Structural, optoelectronic, mechanical, thermodynamic and thermoelectric properties of kesterite Cu2ZnSnS4: A first-principles study
authors: Iskandar Raufzoda, Amondulloi Burhonzoda, Dilshod Nematov, Makhmadzoir Kayumov, Saidjafar Murodzoda, Anushervon Ashurov, Sakhidod Sattorzoda, Makhsud Barot Islomzoda, Kholmirzo Kholmurodov, Shuwei Tang
abstract: arXiv:2611.28172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The structural, optoelectronic, mechanical, thermodynamic, and thermoelectric properties of kesterite Cu2ZnSnS4 were investigated using density functional theory. The mBJ and HSE06 approaches yield band gaps of 0.88 and 1.55 eV, respectively. Optical calculations reveal high absorption, with the onset in the 0.8-1.0 eV range. Hydrostatic compression from 0 to 30 kbar decreases the lattice parameters and increases the band gap. The elastic constants satisfy the Born stability criterion, and B/G $>$ 1.75 indicates plastic behavior. Phonon calculations confirm dynamic stability. In the temperature range from 0 to 1000 K, the Helmholtz free energy decreases, the vibrational entropy increases, and the heat capacity approaches a plateau above 500 K. The thermoelectric properties were investigated in the temperature range from 100 to 1000 K. The Seebeck coefficient remains positive, peaking at approximately 310 $\mu$V/K at 250 K and decreasing to 239 $\mu$V/K at 1000 K. These results encourage the investigation of Cu2ZnSnS4 as a good candidate for thermoelectric power conversion.
summary:
- Band gaps 88 eV (mBJ) and 55 eV (HSE; absorption onset 8–0 eV, high optical absorption.
- Elastic constants satisfy Born stability; B/G > 75 indicates plastic behavior; phonon spectrum confirms dynamic stability.
- Thermoelectric: Seebeck coefficient peaks ~310 µ

title: Physically Informed Data-Driven Modeling of Low-Pressure Carburizing (LPC): A Self-Calibrating Boundary Condition for Carbon Flux
authors: Alex V. Sagalovych, Tymofii Sagalovych, S. F. Dudnik, Vladislav Sagalovych
abstract: arXiv:2611.28190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper formulates an extended framework for a hybrid physically informed data-driven model of low-pressure carburizing (LPC), in which diffusive carbon transport in austenite is described by a physical equation, whereas the effective carbon flux across the gas-metal interface is treated as an unknown boundary forcing to be identified from experimental and process data. The basis for this formulation is that, in LPC, the most uncertain part of the model is not bulk diffusion but the transient surface kinetics of carbon uptake by the metal. In contrast to direct empirical relationships of the 'process regime-result' type, the proposed scheme uses machine learning as a closure operator for the boundary condition in the diffusion problem. This operator is calibrated using carbon concentration profiles, integral mass gain, surface concentration, effective case depth, and additional process measurements. Theoretically, the model is positioned as an operator-learning problem in a system constrained by a partial differential equation, physical flux constraints, inverse-problem regularization, and uncertainty quantification. The relationships between the proposed approach and physics-informed neural networks, operator learning, dynamic-system identification, boundary-operator learning, and boundary-control problems are considered. The mathematical formulation, calibration functional, identifiability conditions, preliminary tuning algorithm, and online adaptation scheme are formulated. The proposed approach is considered as a computational basis for developing interpretable digital support for LPC processes.
summary:
- Hybrid model couples a physical diffusion PDE with a machine‑learning‑identified boundary flux for low‑pressure carburizing.
- Calibrates the boundary operator using experimental concentration profiles, mass gain, surface concentration, and case depth via inverse‑problem regularization.
- Formulated as an operator‑learning problem constrained by PDE physics, flux limits, and uncertainty quantification, linking to PINNs and boundary‑control theory.

title: Defect Engineering of the Water-Carbon Interface: Insights from First-Principles Calculations
authors: Peikun Zhang, Hongbo Zhang, Ying Xu, Zhuhua Zhang
abstract: arXiv:2611.28201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactions at solid-liquid interfaces are fundamental to hydrovoltaic and catalytic technologies. While carbon nanomaterials have been extensively studied, the role of abundant defects in amorphous carbon remains poorly understood. Here, using first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate how various defects (topological, point, line, edge, and doping defects) modulate water-carbon interactions. We find that armchair-edge defects with dangling bonds reduce the energy barrier for water dissociation by up to 30 times compared with pristine carbon, while di-vacancies exhibit a near-zero Gibbs free energy for hydrogen evolution, enabling potential hydrogen evolution reaction activity on a purely carbon-based interface. Moreover, mono-vacancy defects, characterized by reduced electronic localization, enhance charge transfer to evaporating water molecules by up to 12.4 times, a key factor in evaporation-induced electricity generation. Crucially, we demonstrate that coupling distinct defects produces synergistic effects that outperform individual defects, revealing a promising strategy for designing multifunctional interfaces. These insights establish a defect-engineering framework for the rational design of high-efficiency hydrovoltaic and catalytic devices.
summary:
- Armchair-edge dangling bonds cut water‑dissociation barriers ~30×; di‑vacancies give near‑zero Gibbs free energy for H₂ evolution, enabling carbon‑only HER.
- Mono‑vacancies reduce electronic localization, boosting charge transfer to evaporating water up to 4×, aiding evaporation‑induced electricity.
- Coupling different defects produces synergistic effects that outperform single defects, guiding design of multifunctional hydrovoltaic/catalytic interfaces.

title: Multiorbital driving of quantum geometric nonlinear transport in oxide interfaces
authors: Irene Gaiardoni, Mattia Trama, Roberta Citro, Annika Johansson
abstract: arXiv:2611.28213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum geometry plays a relevant role in determining the intrinsic non-linear transport properties of low-dimensional electron systems. Here, we theoretically investigate the quantum geometric contribution to the non-linear conductivity in $\text{SrTiO}_3$-based two-dimensional electron gases, comparing the prototypical (001) and (111) crystallographic interface orientations. Using a multi-orbital tight-binding approach, we uncover the crucial role of the multiband electronic structure in determining the quantum-geometric contribution to nonlinear transport. In particular, we show how the hybridization of $t_{2g}$ orbitals near avoided band crossings shapes the momentum-space distribution of the band-normalized quantum metric and the resulting nonlinear conductivity. Furthermore, we reveal a strong dependence on crystal orientation: while the (001) interface exhibits sharp peak-and-dip features confined around Lifshitz transitions, the trigonal symmetry of the (111) interface promotes strong orbital mixing. Our results highlight how the interplay between orbital hybridization and crystallographic orientation gives rise to distinct quantum-geometric nonlinear transport responses in oxide interfaces.
summary:
- Quantum‑geometric nonlinear conductivity in SrTiO₃ 2DEGs is modeled with a multiorbital tight‑binding Hamiltonian.
- Hybridization of \(t_{2g}\) orbitals near avoided band crossings dictates the momentum‑space quantum metric and the resulting nonlinear response.
- Crystal orientation strongly influences the effect: (interfaces show sharp peak‑dip features at Lifshitz transitions, while (trigonal symmetry enhances orbital mixing and yields a distinct nonlinear transport signature.

title: Nonequilibrium fluctuations could explain the hot mitochondria paradox
authors: Matthew P. Leighton, Benjamin B. Machta
abstract: arXiv:2611.28225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several different experiments have found apparent temperature differences of up to 10 K between the interior of mitochondria and the rest of the cellular environment. The physics of heat conduction, however, precludes the steady-state existence of a temperature difference greater than the microkelvin scale within the cell, absent a far greater energy budget. Nearly a decade after the first reported measurement, this apparent paradox remains unexplained. Here, we propose an explanation which allows the elevated temperature measurements to coexist with the theoretical impossibility of a true 10 K steady-state temperature difference. We suggest that nonequilibrium fluctuations within the cellular environment, combined with molecular temperature probes sensitive to specific ranges of frequencies, can lead to apparent 10 K temperature differences with a biologically attainable power budget.
summary:
- Experiments report ~10 K temperature differences between mitochondria and cytosol, contradicting heat conduction limits.
- The paper proposes nonequilibrium thermal fluctuations plus frequency‑sensitive probes explain apparent temperature spikes.
- This mechanism reconciles observed data with realistic cellular energy budgets.

title: Metal to Semiconductor Transition in Niobium Sulfoselenide Alloy Films by Compositional Control
authors: Tinsae Alem, Abir Hasan, Jordan A. Hachtel, Kory Burns, Nikhil Shukla, Stephen McDonnell
abstract: arXiv:2611.28238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered significant interest due to their tunable bandgaps, optical anisotropy, and mechanical flexibility. This study explores the relationship between stoichiometry, structural phase, and electronic transport in niobium sulfoselenide (NbSxSe2-x) thin films. In this study, low-dimensional TMD films were grown with molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) to investigate the effects of varying chalcogen (sulfur and selenium) content in NbSxSe2-x alloys. We focus on tuning electrical resistivity along with the transition from metallic-to-semiconducting behavior through compositional control. These MBE grown films were characterized using in-vacuo x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze the chemical composition. Electrical resistivity of the films and their temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) were extracted to determine their metallic and semiconducting behavior. Our results show that increasing sulfur content induces a transition from metallic to semiconducting behavior in NbSe2, accompanied by a rise in resistivity. This work highlights the potential for compositional tuning of TMDs for applications in tunable nanoelectronics.
summary:
- MBE-grown NbSₓSe₂₋ₓ films exhibit tunable electronic transport by varying S/Se ratio.
- Higher sulfur content induces a metal‑to‑semiconductor transition, increasing resistivity and TCR.
- In‑vacuo XPS confirms stoichiometry, highlighting compositional control for nanoelectronic applications.

title: Symmetry classes of hyperdeterminant wavefunctions: Application to phase transitions between a bosonic fractional Chern insulator and superfluids
authors: Guan-Lin Lin, Xiaodong Hu, Di Xiao, Ying Ran
abstract: arXiv:2611.28276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a phase transition between a superfluid phase and a fractional Chern insulator phase in a hard-core boson model on the honeycomb lattice using symmetric hyperdeterminant (Hdet) wavefunctions. Combining projective symmetry group analysis with variational Monte Carlo, we construct and optimize Hdet states in various symmetry classes. Based on the associated effective theories, we show that different symmetry classes, i.e., representations of the projective symmetry group, describe specific quantum phases. Compared with traditional fermionic parton construction, the symmetric Hdet wavefunctions are shown to improve microscopics significantly, allowing quantitative investigation of quantum phase diagrams. We argue that, in contrast with the common belief, this putative continuous phase transition is described by a fluctuating $SU(2)_g$ gauge field coupling with four Dirac nodes forming two $SU(2)_g$ doublets (i.e., $N_f=2$ QCD).
summary:
- Employs symmetric hyperdeterminant wavefunctions to model the superfluid–fractional Chern insulator transition in hard‑core bosons on a honeycomb lattice.
- Uses PSG analysis and variational Monte Carlo to classify symmetry classes that correspond to distinct quantum phases, outperforming traditional fermionic parton approaches.
- Proposes the transition is continuous, governed by an SU(\_g gauge field coupled to two Dirac doublets (N\_f = 2 QCD).

title: Intertwined Magneto-Structural Criticality Driving Heterogeneous Collective-Pseudospin Dynamics in Sr2IrO4
authors: Arnab Singh, Junyoung Kwon, AM Milinda Abeykoon
abstract: arXiv:2611.28395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Correlated quantum phenomena arising from spin-orbit-coupled degrees of freedom provide foundational paradigms in emerging quantum technologies and spin-based functionalities. Elucidating the cooperative behaviors of these systems requires a precise probing of their intertwined magnetic and structural configurations. Using complementary resonant X-ray diffraction and high-energy total scattering measurements on single crystals of Sr2IrO4, we observe that spontaneous structural distortions scale quadratically with the magnetic order parameter. Importantly, the lattice distortion inherits the characteristic 2D XY -like critical behavior of the underlying antiferromagnetic order. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) reveals multiscale, temperature- and wave-vector-dependent magnetic dynamics characterized by compressed-exponential relaxation and signatures of critical slowing down near the magnetic transition. These findings suggest the role of spin-orbit coupling and local structural distortions as the possible mechanism orchestrating such unconventional dynamics.
summary:
- Structural distortions scale quadratically with magnetic order, mirroring 2D XY criticality.
- XPCS reveals compressed‑exponential, multiscale magnetic dynamics with critical slowing down near the transition.
- Spin‑orbit coupling and local lattice distortions likely orchestrate the unconventional pseudospin behavior.

title: Competing magnetic correlations in the square-lattice Hubbard model with spin-dependent nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor hopping
authors: Rana Imran Mushtaq, Ji Liu, Yinlong Li, Wing Chi Yu, Xiaosen Yang, Ho-Kin Tang
abstract: arXiv:2611.28593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Altermagnets have spin-split bands without net magnetization. The splitting can come from a spin-dependent nearest-neighbor (NN) hopping anisotropy $t_A$ or from a spin-dependent next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) hopping $t'$. Both change sign under a $90^\circ$ rotation and are present together when the lattice has no mirror planes, yet they have so far been studied only separately. Here we study the two-dimensional square-lattice Hubbard model with both $t_A$ and $t'$, using constrained-path quantum Monte Carlo at $U=4t$ and scanning the electron filling $n$, $t_A$ and $t'$. We find four types of magnetic correlations: N\'eel, stripe, diagonal, and spiral spin-density-wave. The phase diagram depends on both hoppings together. Diagonal correlations require finite $t_A$ and are suppressed by $t'$. Stripe correlations appear only once $t'$ is large enough to overcome the diagonal tendency set by $t_A$. N\'eel correlations survive at large $t_A$ and large $t'$, where the NNN model alone gives stripe or spiral correlations. The noninteracting susceptibility matches the dominant wavevector at small $t'$, but not the N\'eel correlations at $t'\geq0.3$, which come from the interaction. Finite-size scaling with three lattice sizes is consistent with long-range order only near half filling; at the stripe, spiral and diagonal points we tested, the structure factor per site extrapolates to zero. The joint behavior persists up to $U=6t$.
summary:
- Studied the square‑lattice Hubbard model with spin‑dependent NN anisotropy \(t_A\) and NNN hopping \(t'\), finding four magnetic phases (Néel, stripe, diagonal, spiral) whose presence depends on both hoppings.
- Diagonal order requires finite \(t_A\) and is suppressed by \(t'\); stripe order appears only when \(t'\) overcomes the diagonal tendency set by \(t_A\); Néel order survives at large \(t_A\) and \(t'\).

title: Hartree--Fock analysis of the bilayer Hubbard model
abstract: arXiv:2611.28597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the half-filled Hubbard model on two parallel square lattices with on-site repulsion $U>0$ and with nearest-neighbor hopping specified by a constant $t>0$ within each plane and by another constant $t_\perp \geq 0$ between the planes. Working in the Hartree--Fock approximation, we obtain asymptotic formulas for the N\'eel temperature and the antiferromagnetic gap ratio in the weak coupling limit. We also determine the behavior of the antiferromagnetic gap ratio near the critical curve separating the paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic regions in the phase diagram. Furthermore, we present numerical phase diagrams away from half-filling, and we make an analytical conjecture regarding their structure.
summary:
- Hartree–Fock analysis of the half‑filled bilayer Hubbard model with intra‑plane hopping \(t\) and inter‑plane hopping \(t_\perp\).
- Weak‑coupling asymptotic formulas for the Néel temperature and antiferromagnetic gap ratio, plus behavior near the paramagnetic–antiferromagnetic critical curve.
- Numerical phase diagrams away from half‑filling and an analytic conjecture on their overall structure.

title: Observation of nonadiabatic quantum tunneling in a driven correlated insulator
authors: Mingyao Guo, Radu Andrei, Jaena Park, Je-Geun Park, Eugene Demler, David Hsieh
abstract: arXiv:2611.28980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many emerging solid-state platforms for Floquet engineering, nonlinear transport, and high harmonic generation operate near the Keldysh crossover, where optical fields are sufficiently strong and fast to reshape electronic states on sub-cycle timescales. Despite its importance, the microscopic pathways for photocarrier generation in this regime remain poorly understood, as neither perturbative multiphoton absorption nor adiabatic tunneling provides an adequate description. Here, we perform time-resolved optical spectroscopy on the correlated van der Waals insulator NiPS$_3$ while systematically tuning the drive electric field and frequency over a wide range. In the crossover regime, we observe multiphoton-like resonances that are blue-shifted by ponderomotive effects within an otherwise tunneling-dominated absorption channel - a clear spectroscopic signature of adiabaticity breakdown. Hubbard-model simulations based on a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach qualitatively reproduce these features. Together, our results elucidate the microscopic mechanisms of charge excitation in the Keldysh crossover regime and identify a key ingredient for controlling strong-field nonlinear dynamics in correlated materials.
summary:
- Nonadiabatic quantum tunneling observed in NiPS₃ across the Keldysh crossover.
- Blue‑shifted multiphoton resonances appear from ponderomotive effects within a tunneling‑dominated absorption channel.
- Time‑dependent Gaussian variational Hubbard‑model simulations reproduce the spectroscopic signatures, clarifying charge‑excitation pathways.

title: Finite-size reversal of a multiparticle correction to local spin spectra in a flux-disordered Kitaev honeycomb model
abstract: arXiv:2611.29070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A spin flip in the Kitaev honeycomb model changes the flux background and therefore the Hamiltonian seen by the matter fermions. Can a one-particle approximation with the correct total spin intensity nevertheless misestimate the depth of a depression in the local spin spectrum? We test this question in a frozen, flux-disordered ensemble by retaining the actual one-particle transition energies and relative spectral weights after the spin flip, then rescaling those weights to match the full intensity. We measure the depression by subtracting the central intensity from the average at two flanking frequencies. For spin-created states with odd final quasiparticle number and nonzero one-particle weight, restoring multiparticle weight shallows the depression on 24 sites and deepens it on both 1,536-site shapes and the 3,456- and 6,144-site tori, as judged by the median paired correction at each of two energy resolutions. For these states, the one-particle approximation overestimates the mean dip depth by about 16-18% on 24 sites and underestimates it by 33-56% in the 6,144-site sample. Extrapolating from 24 sites would therefore give the wrong sign for this correction on those four larger tori under the same disorder prescription.
summary:
- Assesses one‑particle vs. multiparticle effects on local spin‑spectra depressions in flux‑disordered Kitaev honeycomb model.
- Restoring multiparticle weight shallowens the dip on 24 sites but deepens it on 1,536–6,144‑site lattices.
- One‑particle approximation overestimates dip depth by ~16–18 % on small systems and underestimates it by 33–56 % on large systems, causing sign errors when extrapolating.

title: A Fiber-Optic Platform for Cryogenic Laser-Pump Neutron-Probe Magneto-Optical Measurements
authors: Lazar L. Kish, Andrei T. Savici, Tyler K. White, Vlad N. Sedov, Andrey A. Podlesnyak, Matthias D. Frontzek, Barry L. Winn, Igor A. Zaliznyak
abstract: arXiv:2611.29114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report a fiber-optic laser-pump neutron-probe method for momentum- and frequency-resolved magneto-optical measurements. The technique uses inelastic neutron scattering to measure time-dependent two-point magnetization correlations, S(Q,$\omega$), after resonant photoexcitation at cryogenic temperatures. We demonstrate it by measuring nonequilibrium thermalization dynamics in Yb-based quantum magnets.
summary:
- Fiber‑optic laser‑pump neutron‑probe technique for momentum‑ and frequency‑resolved magneto‑optical measurements.
- Measures time‑dependent two‑point magnetization correlations S(Q, ω) via inelastic neutron scattering after resonant photoexcitation at cryogenic temperatures.
- Demonstrated on nonequilibrium thermalization dynamics in Yb‑based quantum magnets.

title: Quantum-Metric-Driven Hollow Wigner Crystals
abstract: arXiv:2611.29317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies have revealed the profound influence of Berry curvature on electron crystallization, yet the independent role of the quantum metric remains unclear. Here, we introduce a minimal three-band continuum model with separately tunable quantum metric and Berry flux. Employing the Hartree-Fock approach, we find that a conventional s-wave Wigner crystal can develop a hollow charge distribution with depleted density at lattice sites, without a change in symmetry or topology. We show that this density reconstruction occurs even at vanishing Berry curvature and arises from strong quantum metric and the nontrivial angular structure of the form factor. In our model, the continuous crossover between hollow and conventional WCs is accompanied by anomalous direct exchange interactions, nearly vanishing at intermediate quantum metric but enhanced by over an order of magnitude in the strong-metric regime. These results reveal how quantum metric can reshape both the charge distribution and exchange interactions of electron crystals beyond simple wave-function delocalization.
summary:
- Quantum metric alone can turn a conventional s‑wave Wigner crystal into a hollow charge distribution, even with zero Berry curvature.
- The hollow‑to‑conventional crossover is continuous and accompanied by anomalous direct exchange interactions.
- In the strong‑metric regime, exchange interactions increase by over an order of magnitude, reshaping charge distribution beyond simple delocalization.

title: Ground-State Manifold Curvature and Phase Transitions in the Kitaev Honeycomb Model
authors: Omid Yahyayi Monem, Setare Bashari, Hosein Mohammadzadeh
abstract: arXiv:2611.29495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Kitaev honeycomb model is an exactly solvable spin model whose ground state realizes a quantum spin liquid with gapped Abelian phases and a gapless phase that becomes a non-Abelian phase in a magnetic field. Here we study its phase transitions through the geometry of the ground-state manifold, using the Ricci scalar of the quantum metric. In the three gapped phases we obtain closed-form expressions for the curvature, which is negative and diverges at the critical lines; the three phases are related to one another by an exact change of coordinates. In the gapless phase, the curvature of the infrared-regularized metric is positive and decays inversely with the logarithm of the system size, with a size-independent amplitude that diverges at the phase boundaries, with an exponent different from that of the gapped side. The change of sign and the divergences together reproduce the complete phase diagram. A magnetic field gaps out the gapless phase and plays the role of the infrared cutoff, so that away from the critical lines the curvature of the non-Abelian phase becomes finite and positive, while around the critical lines it opens a crossover region whose width scales quadratically with the field. Since divergences of geometric quantities are often regarded as signatures of phase transitions, the divergence of the Ricci scalar at the critical lines provides a geometric signature of these transitions.
summary:
- Ricci scalar of the quantum metric diverges negatively at critical lines between the three gapped phases, with closed‑form expressions related by coordinate changes.
- In the gapless phase the curvature is positive, decays as \(1/\ln L\), diverges at boundaries with a distinct exponent, and a magnetic field introduces a finite IR cutoff yielding positive curvature and a quadratic‑width crossover.
- The divergence of the Ricci scalar thus serves as a geometric signature of all phase transitions in the Kitaev honeycomb model.
